title: `Chat$chat()` docs don't list possible `echo` values, and `$chat_structured()` recommends deprecated `echo = "text"`
body: The `echo` parameter on `Chat$chat()` says "whether to emit the response to stdout as it is received" but doesn't list the possible values; they're only enumerated on the `Chat` constructor. `$chat_structured()` and `$chat_structured_async()` tell users to set `echo = "text"`, which `check_echo()` has treated as deprecated in favour of `"output"` since 0.2.0. Suggest listing `"none"`, `"output"`, and `"all"` on `$chat()` and replacing `"text"` with `"output"` in the structured methods.

title: parallel_chat_structured() silently drops include_tokens and include_cost for an array type
body:
## Summary

`parallel_chat_structured(include_tokens = TRUE, include_cost = TRUE)` silently returns no token counts and no cost when `type` is a `type_array()`. Both flags are accepted and ignored.

## Why

`multi_convert()` attaches usage only when the converted result is a data frame:

```r
if (convert) {
  out <- convert_from_type(row_data, type_array(type))
}
...
if (is.data.frame(out)) {
  ...
  if (include_tokens) { out$input_tokens <- ...; out$output_tokens <- ...; out$cached_input_tokens <- ... }
  if (include_cost)   { out$cost <- ... }
}
out
```

For an array `type`, `convert_from_type(row_data, type_array(type))` is a `type_array(type_array(...))` conversion and returns a plain list of tibbles, one per prompt, so `is.data.frame(out)` is `FALSE` and the block is skipped. There is no warning that the request could not be honoured. (`convert = FALSE` returns a bare list too, so it has the same gap.)

## Reproducible shape, without a provider

The branch is decided by what `convert_from_type()` returns:

```r
items <- type_object(text = type_string(), label = type_string())
rows  <- list(list(list(text = "a", label = "x")), list(list(text = "b", label = "y")))

is.data.frame(ellmer:::convert_from_type(rows, type_array(type_array(items = items))))
#> FALSE   -> usage columns never attached

wrapped <- type_object(items = type_array(items = items))
rows2   <- lapply(rows, function(r) list(items = r))
is.data.frame(ellmer:::convert_from_type(rows2, type_array(wrapped)))
#> TRUE    -> usage columns attached beside a list-column
```

Live, `parallel_chat_structured(chat, prompts, type = type_array(items = items), include_cost = TRUE)` returns the list with no `cost` anywhere. ellmer 0.4.2.

## Suggestions

Either of these would do:

- Attach usage for a list result as well, e.g. as attributes on the list, or by returning a tibble with a list-column for array types when usage is requested.
- Or refuse the flags for array types with an error, so the caller learns at the call rather than by noticing an absence.

## Context

Found in quallmer (quallmer/quallmer#119), whose `qlm_segment()` asks for an array of segments per document and could not cost a run. Our workaround is to request `type_object(segments = type_array(...))` instead, which converts to one row per prompt with the usage beside the list-column, matching the wrapping ellmer does internally for providers that require an object at the top level.

title: Support `defer_loading` and tool search, now shipped by both Anthropic and OpenAI
body:
An app with a large tool set pays for every tool schema on every request, and `ellmer` offers no way to avoid it short of registering and unregistering tools mid-conversation. That workaround is worse than the problem: tools render ahead of `system` and `messages`, so changing the tool set invalidates the prompt cache for the entire request — the manifest, the system prompt and every turn of history.

## Both providers now solve this, and agree on the spelling

Anthropic and OpenAI have each shipped deferred tool loading, using the same field name. A tool marked `defer_loading: true` is declared but its schema is not loaded into context; a search tool loads the ones the model actually needs.

- Anthropic takes `defer_loading` as an optional property on a tool definition, alongside `cache_control`, `strict` and `allowed_callers`, paired with `tool_search_tool_regex_20251119` or the BM25 variant.
- OpenAI takes the same `defer_loading: true` flag with `{"type": "tool_search"}` in the tools array, on the Responses API, for `gpt-5.4` and later.

Both place the loaded definitions at the end of the context specifically to protect the cache. From Azure's write-up of the OpenAI feature: *"Both hosted and client-executed tool search load tools at the end of the model's context window. This placement preserves the model's cache between requests."* Its troubleshooting table names the failure this issue is about — *"Prompt caching stops at a tool update … Keep prior items stable and append newly loaded tools at the end of the context."*

Google has no equivalent, so this covers two of the three major providers rather than all of them.

## Most of the machinery is already there

The search tool itself needs nothing new conceptually. A `ToolBuiltIn` already carries a raw `json` slot that the provider methods pass straight through — `as_json()` for `ToolBuiltIn` on Anthropic is just `x@json` — and `claude_tool_web_search()`, `openai_tool_web_search()` and `google_tool_web_fetch()` are that pattern in use. A `claude_tool_search()` / `openai_tool_search()` pair would be one more entry in the family.

The missing half is the flag on ordinary tools. A `ToolDef` serialises to exactly `list(name, description, input_schema)` for Anthropic, with no channel for an extra field. The `annotations` slot exists but is not rendered, and `api_args` cannot reach it either: `modify_list()` is `utils::modifyList()`, so a `tools` key already set by `chat_body()` is merged rather than replaced, and the recursion over two unnamed lists is a silent no-op.

## Why this is safe to expose in a cross-provider API

A deferred tool is still declared and still callable — the flag governs only whether its schema is loaded up front. A provider that does not support deferral can ignore the flag and behave exactly as it does today, losing the token saving and nothing else. The abstraction therefore degrades honestly rather than becoming a no-op that quietly means something different per provider, which is the usual reason to keep a vendor feature out of a shared API.

## Proposed shape

A `defer_loading` argument on `tool()`, rendered by the providers that understand it and dropped by those that do not, plus `claude_tool_search()` and `openai_tool_search()` alongside the existing built-in tool constructors.

If a per-tool passthrough is preferred over a named argument, that would also reach `cache_control`, `strict` and `allowed_callers`, which are unreachable today for the same reason — `ToolBuiltIn@json` is the precedent for what that would look like on a `ToolDef`.

One implementation note: tool search introduces `tool_search_call` and `tool_search_output` items in the Responses output, so the turn parser needs to tolerate them. That overlaps with #928.

Happy to open a PR if this is a direction you would take.

title: Make date format prompt unambiguous in `test_tools_simple()`
body: Running the live Databricks tests with the new default model (`databricks-claude-sonnet-5`), the "supports tool calling" test failed because the model reformatted the tool result "2024-01-01" as "2024-1-1" in its reply. The `test_tools_simple()` helper in `tests/testthat/helper-provider.R` asks for the date "in Y-M-D format", which doesn't say anything about zero padding, but then uses `expect_match(result, "2024-01-01")`. Asking for "YYYY-MM-DD format" instead should make the expected output unambiguous without loosening the check.

title: `parallel_chat_structured()` returns an ordinary row, with no `.error`, for a response cut off at `max_tokens`
body:
## Summary

`chat_structured()` raises an error when a response is truncated (#867, since 0.4.2), via `check_finish_reason()`. `parallel_chat_structured()` and `batch_chat_structured()` do not. `parallel_turns()` builds the turns and `multi_convert()` converts them without looking at `turn@finish_reason`, so a response that hit `max_tokens` comes back as an ordinary row: `NA` scalars, or a zero-row tibble for an array property, no `.error`, and the request billed in full. The turns are then discarded, so the caller cannot recover the finish reason afterwards.

The finish reason is available on the turn the whole time. Running the same request through `parallel_chat()` and reading `last_turn()@finish_reason` gives `"max_tokens"` in every case below.

## Reprex

Three providers, one prompt that cannot fit in 60 output tokens. For each: `parallel_chat_structured()` on the request, then the finish reason of the same request via `parallel_chat()`, then `chat_structured()` on it.

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(ellmer))
type <- type_object(items = type_array(type_object(name = type_string(), why = type_string())))
prompt <- "List 25 fruits, each with a two-sentence reason it is healthy."
probe <- function(chat_fn, label, ...) {
  cat("\n\n########", label, "########\n")
  ch <- chat_fn(..., params = params(max_tokens = 60))
  res <- tryCatch(parallel_chat_structured(ch, list(prompt), type, include_tokens = TRUE),
                  error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(res, "error")) cat("ERROR:", conditionMessage(res), "\n") else print(res)
  chs <- parallel_chat(ch, list(prompt))
  t <- chs[[1]]$last_turn(); cat("finish_reason:", t@finish_reason, " tokens:", t@tokens, "\n")
  r <- tryCatch(ch$clone()$chat_structured(prompt, type = type), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(r, "condition")) cat(class(r)[1], ":", conditionMessage(r), "\n") else str(r)
}
probe(chat_anthropic, "anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5", model = "claude-haiku-4-5")
#> 
#> 
#> ######## anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5 ########
#> Warning: Failed to extract data from 1/1 turns
#> * 1: parse error: premature EOF {"items": [{"name": "Apple", "w (right here)
#> ------^
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   items            input_tokens output_tokens cached_input_tokens
#>   <list>                  <dbl>         <dbl>               <dbl>
#> 1 <tibble [0 × 2]>          281            60                   0
#> finish_reason: max_tokens  tokens: 24 60 0 
#> rlang_error : Response was truncated because it hit the `max_tokens` limit.
#> ℹ Increase `max_tokens` to allow the model to generate the full response.
probe(chat_anthropic, "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5", model = "claude-sonnet-5")
#> 
#> 
#> ######## anthropic/claude-sonnet-5 ########
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   items            input_tokens output_tokens cached_input_tokens
#>   <list>                  <dbl>         <dbl>               <dbl>
#> 1 <tibble [0 × 2]>          725            60                   0
#> finish_reason: max_tokens  tokens: 30 60 0 
#> rlang_error : Response was truncated because it hit the `max_tokens` limit.
#> ℹ Increase `max_tokens` to allow the model to generate the full response.
probe(chat_openai, "openai/gpt-5-mini", model = "gpt-5-mini")
#> 
#> 
#> ######## openai/gpt-5-mini ########
#> Warning: Failed to extract data from 1/1 turns
#> * 1: Data extraction failed: no JSON responses found.
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   items            input_tokens output_tokens cached_input_tokens
#>   <list>                  <dbl>         <dbl>               <dbl>
#> 1 <tibble [0 × 2]>           79             0                   0
#> finish_reason: max_tokens  tokens: 22 0 0 
#> rlang_error : Response was truncated because it hit the `max_tokens` limit.
#> ℹ Increase `max_tokens` to allow the model to generate the full response.
```

<sup>Created on 2026-09-03 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

## What the run shows

In all three cases the turn's finish reason is `max_tokens`, `chat_structured()` raises, and `parallel_chat_structured()` returns a one-row tibble with a zero-row `items` and no `.error` column. The details differ by provider, and none of them gives the caller a reliable signal:

- **claude-haiku-4-5** warns "Failed to extract data ... premature EOF", because the cut-off JSON does not parse. The warning is the only trace; the row itself carries nothing.
- **claude-sonnet-5** warns nothing at all. The truncated tool call arrives with an empty `input`, which converts cleanly to an empty array. (See the note on `has_claude_structured_output()` below for why this model takes the tool path.)
- **gpt-5-mini** warns "no JSON responses found", and reports `output_tokens` of 0 because the budget went on reasoning, so even the token count does not reveal a cut.

For a schema where an empty array is a legitimate answer, a truncated response is indistinguishable from "nothing found", and the inputs affected are systematically the longest ones. The same holds for `batch_chat_structured()`, which converts through the same `multi_convert()`.

## Suggestion

Apply the same per-turn check on the parallel and batch paths, with the outcome `on_error = "continue"` already implies for a failed request: a turn whose finish reason is `max_tokens`, `context_window` or `content_filter` is treated as failed in `multi_convert()`, so the row gets `NA` values and an `.error` carrying the condition `check_finish_reason()` would have raised. Or, more generally, return the turns (or their finish reasons) alongside the converted table, so the caller can decide.

This is a sibling of #1121, which asks for extraction failures to be recorded in `.error`. That change would cover the Haiku and OpenAI cases above, where extraction fails, but not the Sonnet case, where the truncated payload extracts cleanly, nor a response cut off just after producing valid JSON. Both changes need the same hook, the point in `multi_convert()` where the turns are still in hand.

## A related observation

`has_claude_structured_output()` matches `^claude-\w+-4-[5-9]`, so `claude-sonnet-5` and `claude-opus-5` take the forced-tool path rather than native structured output. That is why the truncated Sonnet response above produces an empty `input` rather than a parse error.

Context: [quallmer](https://github.com/quallmer/quallmer) reports per-unit failures from `.error` and needed this for quallmer/quallmer#153. Our interim fix infers a cut from `include_tokens` when the caller declared `max_tokens` itself, which cannot see a provider default limit. Happy to send a PR if the direction is acceptable.

title: `multi_convert()` drops extraction failures instead of recording them in `.error`
body:
`parallel_chat_structured()` and `batch_chat_structured()` record request failures in an `.error` column, as documented: "If the output is a data frame, and some requests error, an `.error` column will be added with the error objects." But a request that *succeeds* and returns a turn from which no structured data can be extracted (a refusal in prose, a truncated response, a model that ignored the schema) is handled differently: `multi_convert()` reports it in a warning listing the affected rows, then drops the condition. The row comes back with `NA` scalars, or a zero-length cell for an array, and `.error` is `NULL` there.

For scalar properties a caller can still infer the failure from the `NA`s. For a property that is a `type_array()`, they cannot: after conversion, a failed extraction and a valid empty array are the same zero-row tibble. The only record that anything went wrong is the text of a warning that has already been emitted.

## Reprex

Uses the internal `multi_convert()` directly so it runs offline, since that is where both kinds of failure meet. `ContentJson` is internal too; it stands in for what a successful structured response carries.

```r
library(ellmer)
packageVersion("ellmer")
#> [1] '0.4.2'

provider <- chat_openai(credentials = function() list(Authorization = "Bearer x"))$get_provider()
#> Using model = "gpt-5.4".

type <- type_object(
  assessments = type_array(items = type_object(item = type_string(), score = type_integer()))
)

# Three turns: one good, one that came back as prose, one whose request failed
good   <- AssistantTurn(contents = list(ellmer:::ContentJson(list(assessments = list(list(item = "apples", score = 2L))))))
prose  <- AssistantTurn(contents = list(ContentText("I am sorry, I cannot score this text.")))
failed <- simpleError("HTTP 429 Too Many Requests")

out <- ellmer:::multi_convert(provider, list(good, prose, failed), type)
#> Warning message:
#> Failed to extract data from 1/3 turns
#> * 2: Data extraction failed: no JSON responses found.

out
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   assessments      .error
#>   <list>           <list>
#> 1 <tibble [1 × 2]> <NULL>
#> 2 <tibble [0 × 2]> <NULL>
#> 3 <tibble [0 × 2]> <smplErrr>

sapply(out$assessments, nrow)
#> [1] 1 0 0
```

Row 3 (request failed) carries its error. Row 2 (request succeeded, extraction failed) is indistinguishable from a row whose model validly returned an empty array, and `.error` says nothing about it.

## Where it happens

In `multi_convert()`, the extraction is wrapped in `safely()` and the condition is used only for the warning:

```r
rows <- map(turns, function(turn) {
  if (turn_failed(turn)) NULL
  else safely(extract_data(turn = turn, type = ..., convert = FALSE, needs_wrapper = needs_wrapper))
})
is_err <- map_lgl(rows, function(x) !is.null(x$error))
if (n_error > 0) {
  msgs <- map(rows[is_err], function(x) conditionMessage(x$error))
  cli::cli_warn(c("Failed to extract data from {n_error}/{length(turns)} turns", ...))
}
row_data <- map(rows, function(x) x$result)
...
is_error <- map_lgl(turns, turn_failed)   # only request failures reach .error
if (any(is_error)) { errors[is_error] <- turns[is_error]; out$.error <- errors }
```

`rows[[i]]$error` is in hand at the point `.error` is built, so recording it there would be a small change.

## Suggestion

Populate `.error` for extraction failures as well as request failures, so the column means "this row has no usable result, and here is why" regardless of which stage failed. The warning can stay. Two details worth deciding:

- Keep the request error when both could apply (they cannot today, since a failed turn is never extracted, but the precedence is worth stating).
- The same applies to `convert = FALSE` only insofar as `.error` is attached at all on that path; currently it is not, since the `.error`/tokens/cost block is inside `if (is.data.frame(out))`.

Context: we hit this in [quallmer](https://github.com/quallmer/quallmer), which reports per-unit failures from `.error` (quallmer/quallmer#132). Our interim fix is a calling handler around the structured call that parses the `* <row>: <message>` lines of the warning back into `.error`, with a test pinned against `multi_convert()` so a format change fails our suite. That works, but it is a reconstruction of information ellmer already had. Happy to send a PR if the direction is acceptable.

title: Assorted provider gaps found while auditing feature support
body:
While auditing feature support across the official providers, 🤖 found a few apparent bugs. Status after investigating each:

- **Confirmed:** `chat_deepseek()` silently drops non-text user content: `as_json(Turn)` (R/provider-deepseek.R:105) keeps only `ContentText`, so images and PDFs are discarded without a warning and the model never sees them. Verified empirically. Images are a documented limitation, but we should error (like Snowflake does) rather than silently drop. Straightforward fix.
- **Confirmed, needs a live check:** `chat_snowflake()` never sets `finish_reason` in `value_turn()` (R/provider-snowflake.R:313) and has no `value_finish_reason` method, so the truncation warnings added in 0.4.2 (#867) can't fire. Caveat: chatlas has the same gap with a `# TODO: no finish_reason in Snowflake?` comment for the same `inference:complete` endpoint, and Snowflake's docs suggest support is patchy (absent entirely for Claude models). Needs a live test to see what the API actually returns before wiring anything up.
- **Confirmed:** `chat_aws_bedrock()` doesn't stream thinking: `stream_content()` (R/provider-aws.R:344) only emits `ContentText` live; `reasoningContent` deltas are accumulated in `stream_merge_chunks()` but never emitted, so thinking only appears in the completed turn. Inconsistent with the direct Claude provider, which streams `ContentThinking` (R/provider-claude.R:323). Straightforward fix.
- **Confirmed unverified inheritance:** `chat_posit()` inherits `has_batch_support = TRUE` from `ProviderAnthropic`, so `batch_chat()` will POST to `{gateway}/anthropic/v1/messages/batches` with no verification that the gateway supports that endpoint. chatlas notes the gateway doesn't proxy the beta Files API, so incomplete endpoint coverage is plausible; chatlas appears to have the same inheritance. Needs a live test against the gateway (or confirmation from Posit folks); if unsupported the fix is a one-line override.
- **Feature gap, not a bug:** `google_upload()` is hardcoded to the Gemini endpoint (R/provider-google-upload.R:31), and this is more than parameterization: Vertex has no Files API equivalent and expects Cloud Storage URIs instead, so Vertex audio/video support is new functionality (e.g. accepting `gs://` URIs). The docs already note it's Gemini specific. Should be split into a separate feature request.

title: Model metadata omits the context window
body:
The `models_*()` functions don't report how much context a model accepts, and nothing on `Chat` exposes it either. A caller can see how many tokens a conversation has accumulated, through `get_tokens()`, but not how close that is to the limit — leaving a hardcoded per-model table that goes stale with every release, or per-provider HTTP calls, as the only ways to find out. That is the work ellmer otherwise saves callers from doing.

Most providers already return it, in a response ellmer parses and then discards. The table below is a brief overview gathered from their docs, so it may well have shifted by the time anyone acts on it.

| Provider | Endpoint | Field |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anthropic | `/v1/models` | `max_input_tokens`, `max_tokens` |
| OpenRouter | `/api/v1/models` | `context_length` |
| Gemini | `/models` | `inputTokenLimit`, `outputTokenLimit` |
| Mistral | `/v1/models` | `max_context_length` |
| vLLM | `/v1/models` | `max_model_len` |
| LM Studio | `/v1/models` | `max_context_length` |
| Ollama | `api/show` | `<arch>.context_length`, not in the `api/tags` ellmer calls |
| OpenAI | `/v1/models` | Absent |
| Bedrock | `ListFoundationModels` | Absent |
| Portkey | `/models` | Absent; normalised to the OpenAI shape before it reaches ellmer |

Five of those are a parser widening — the Anthropic parser keeps `id`, `display_name` and `created_at`, and the vLLM and LM Studio parsers keep `id` alone. Ollama needs a second call. For the last three there is nothing to read, which is what `NA` is for. OpenAI's model object is only `id`, `object`, `created` and `owned_by`, so everyone keeps their own table — including OpenAI, whose Codex CLI [added a `max_context_window` field to its own model metadata](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/18382) in April.

Suggestion: add it to the `models_*()` data frames as `max_input_tokens`, or whatever name generalises best, `NA` where the provider doesn't report it. Exposing it on `Chat` too would pair naturally with `get_tokens()`, and would give the compaction hook in #1051 the number it needs to decide.

Happy to send a PR if you'd like one.

title: consider a Chat field describing whether thinking is enabled
body:

title: Feature Request: Allow custom `base_url` in `chat_google_vertex()` for API gateway proxies
body:
Note: Steps so far were run locally and final issue was created with assistance of Opus 4.6

## Problem

When using Google Vertex AI models through a corporate API gateway (Azure API Management),
the gateway proxies requests using Google's native API format
(`/v1beta1/publishers/google/models/{model}:generateContent`) with API key auth
(`x-goog-api-key` header).

Currently, `chat_google_vertex()` does not accept a `base_url` argument, so there's
no way to point it at a custom endpoint. The gateway is NOT OpenAI-compatible, so
`chat_openai_compatible()` doesn't work either.

## Workaround

Using `httr2` directly works:

```r
url <- "https://my-gateway.example.com/vertex-ai-express/v1beta1/publishers/google/models/gemini-2.5-flash-lite:generateContent"

resp <- request(url) |>
  req_headers(`x-goog-api-key` = api_key, `Content-Type` = "application/json") |>
  req_body_json(list(
    contents = list(list(role = "user", parts = list(list(text = "Hello!"))))
  )) |>
  req_perform()
```

The Python `google.genai` SDK supports this via `HttpOptions(base_url=...)`:

```python
from google.genai import Client
from google.genai.types import HttpOptions

client = Client(vertexai=True, api_key=api_key, http_options=HttpOptions(base_url=ENDPOINT))
```

## Proposed Solution
Add a `base_url` parameter to `chat_google_vertex()` that overrides the default Google endpoint URL, similar to how the Python SDK's `HttpOptions(base_url=...)` works.

This would also need to support API key authentication (via `x-goog-api-key header`) as an alternative to OAuth/service account credentials.

## Environment
* ellmer version: 0.4.1
* R version: [your R version]

title: Tool definitions don't accept valid special characters for function names or arguments, such as "ñ"
body:
R functions that contain characters such as "ñ" (very common Spanish letter that produces a common problem in data science, as its used in the word _año_, meaning _year_) are completely valid in R, but they cause problems with `{ellmer}`

Lets create a basic function that has `ñ` in its name and in its argument:

```r
obtener_datos_por_año <- function(año = NULL) {
  
  require(dplyr)
  
  datos <- data.frame(
    año = c(2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024),
    inversión = c(100, 150, 200, 250, 300),
    proyectos = c(5, 8, 12, 15, 18)
  )
  
  datos <- datos |> 
    filter(año == .env$año)
  
  return(datos)
}
```
The function simply filters data from a dataframe.

Try out the function and it will work fine:

```r
obtener_datos_por_año(año = 2022)
```

Now let's create a tool definition with `{ellmer}`:

```r
library(ellmer)

# Crear la herramienta ellmer
tool_obtener_datos <- ellmer::tool(
  obtener_datos_por_año,
  "Obtiene datos de inversión y proyectos, filtrados opcionalmente por año (2020-2024)",
  arguments = list(
    año = type_integer(description = "Año a filtrar, entre 2020 y 2024")
  )
)
```

We get the first error: `ñ` is not supported in a function name:
```
# Error in `ellmer::tool()`:
#   ! `name` must contain only letters, numbers, - and _.
```

We have to change the function name (let´s say `anio` instead of `año`) to get rid of the error.

Now let's provide the LLM with the function definition:

```r
chat <- chat_anthropic(
  model = "claude-haiku-4-5"
)

chat$register_tool(tool_obtener_datos)
```

No problem so far, but let's ask a question that requires the model to use the tool, specifically the argument with `ñ` in its name:

```
chat$chat("muéstrame los proyectos de 2020") # "show me projects from 2020"
```

We get another `ñ` related error:
```
# Error in `req_perform_connection()`:
#   ! HTTP 400 Bad Request.
# ℹ tools.0.custom.input_schema.properties: Property keys should match
# pattern '^[a-zA-Z0-9_.-]{1,64}$' [invalid_request_error]
# Run `rlang::last_trace()` to see where the error occurred.
```

I believe some cautions were taken to validate proper function and argument names in `{ellmer}` but those leave some users having to modify their work in order to match the english alphabet.

title: Streaming ContentThinking chunks lack proper <thinking> tag boundaries
body:
## Current behavior

When streaming with `stream = "content"`, each `ContentThinking` chunk is yielded as an independent object. If you print or concatenate these (via `format()`), each fragment gets its own `<thinking>...</thinking>` wrapper:

```r
chat <- chat_anthropic(model = "claude-sonnet-4-20250514")

stream <- chat$stream("Explain recursion", stream = "content")
coro::loop(for (chunk in stream) {
  cat(format(chunk))
})
```

Output:

```
<thinking>
The user wants an explanation
</thinking>
<thinking>
 of recursion. I should
</thinking>
<thinking>
 start with a simple definition...
</thinking>
Recursion is a technique where...
```

With `stream = "text"`, thinking text is yielded as bare strings indistinguishable from response text:

```r
stream <- chat$stream("Explain recursion", stream = "text")
coro::loop(for (chunk in stream) {
  cat(chunk)
})
```

Output:

```
The user wants an explanation of recursion. I should start with a simple definition...Recursion is a technique where...
```

No way to tell where thinking ended and the response began.

## Expected behavior

The streaming layer should emit `<thinking>` tags at the boundaries — once at the start of thinking, once at the end — so that concatenated output is well-formed:

For `stream = "text"`:
```
<thinking>
The user wants an explanation of recursion. I should start with a simple definition...
</thinking>

Recursion is a technique where...
```

For `stream = "content"`, the yielded objects stay the same (`ContentThinking` per chunk), but the echo/display output should show proper boundaries.

## Why this matters

Downstream consumers (like shinychat) that receive a stream and need to separate thinking from response content currently have to implement their own stateful tracking of `ContentThinking` objects, accumulate the thinking text, and reconstruct the tag boundaries themselves. If the stream already had correct boundaries in text mode, consumers could treat it as a text stream with well-formed `<thinking>` tags and parse accordingly — no type inspection needed.

title: Token Budget / Cap for Agentic Tool Call Loops
body:
**Describe the problem**
When running unsupervised/scheduled agentic workflows that involve tool calls, there is currently no built-in way to enforce an upper token limit on the full multi-turn loop. Without this, a runaway loop can consume far more tokens than intended with no mechanism to stop it gracefully.

**Desired behavior**
It would be useful to have a supported way to:
1. Set a hard token budget for the entire tool call loop, causing it to stop (and error/fail gracefully) if the limit is exceeded.
2. Optionally inject a system-level message (e.g. *"You are approaching your token limit — wrap up your response now"*) once a soft threshold is reached, giving the model a chance to return a partial result rather than hard-stopping.

**Use case**
Unsupervised scheduled reports with tool access, where cost/token control is a requirement to prevent silent runaway.

title: Support multi-turn conversation suffixes in `parallel_chat_structured()`
body:
### Problem

`parallel_chat_structured()` currently supports only a single user turn per parallel job. This is because `as_user_turns()` converts each element of `prompts` into one `UserTurn`, and `append_turns()` appends that single turn to the shared conversation history:

```r
# R/parallel-chat.R L192-199
user_turns <- as_user_turns(prompts)
existing <- chat$get_turns(include_system_prompt = TRUE)
conversations <- append_turns(list(existing), user_turns)
```

```r
# R/turns.R L219-231
as_user_turns <- function(prompts, ...) {
  turns <- map(seq_along(prompts), function(i) {
    as_user_turn(prompts[[i]], ...)
  })
  turns
}
```

There is no mechanism to supply a multi-turn conversation suffix (e.g., user → assistant → user) per parallel job. Workloads that require each parallel item to be its own short conversation — rather than a single prompt — must fall back to sequential `chat$chat_structured()` calls on separate `Chat` objects, losing the throughput benefit of the parallel API.

### Use case

Simulation-style and survey-style workflows where each parallel item naturally involves multiple turns before the structured extraction. For example, running 500 independent two-turn conversations in parallel:

- **Turn 1:** establish identity/context for a simulated respondent
- **Turn 2:** ask the rating/classification question
- **Return:** structured JSON response

Other examples include multi-step annotation pipelines and interview-style prompting where the model should condition on a short prior exchange before producing a structured answer.

### Proposed API

Allow each element of `prompts` to be either a string (current behaviour, one turn) or a list of strings (new, multi-turn suffix):

```r
parallel_chat_structured(
  chat = chat,
  prompts = list(
    # Job 1: two-turn conversation
    list("You are simulating a Democrat.", "Rate this statement from 0 to 100."),
    # Job 2: two-turn conversation
    list("You are simulating a Republican.", "Rate this statement from 0 to 100."),
    # Job 3: single-turn (backward compatible)
    "Rate this statement from 0 to 100."
  ),
  type = response_type
)
```

This would also apply to `parallel_chat()`, `parallel_chat_text()`, and `batch_chat_structured()` since they share the same `as_user_turns()` / `append_turns()` pipeline.

### Implementation notes

The main changes would likely be in:

- **`as_user_turns()`** (`R/turns.R`): detect when an element is a list of strings and return a list of `Turn` objects (alternating user/assistant) rather than a single `UserTurn`.
- **`append_turns()`** (`R/parallel-chat.R`): handle appending a sequence of turns rather than a single turn.
- **`parallel_chat_structured()`** (`R/parallel-chat.R`): the structured variant would need to issue multiple rounds of `parallel_turns()` calls, similar to how `parallel_chat()` already loops for tool calls.

### Not a bug

The current docs and API clearly treat `prompts` as single-turn inputs. This is a feature request to extend the parallel API to cover multi-turn workloads.

_Originally raised in https://github.com/rempsyc/ellmer/issues/4._

title: Feature Request: Implement Native "Agent" Class (ReAct Loop) for Autonomous Workflows
body:
he Problem: Lack of Autonomy
Currently, `ellmer` provides an excellent interface for one-shot or interactive chat. However, it lacks a native mechanism for autonomy.

To execute multi-step tasks (e.g., "Download this CSV, clean it, and plot the trend"), a user currently has to manually act as the "runtime"—copying code blocks, executing them, and pasting errors back into the chat. There is no persistent object capable of the ReAct (Reason + Act) pattern to handle this loop automatically.

 The Proposed Solution
I propose implementing a dedicated `Agent` class (likely an R6 object) that wraps the existing `Chat` interface to enable autonomous execution.

1. The `Agent` Class (The Brain)
A stateful object that manages a `while` loop of  Thought → Action → Observation.
* It would leverage the existing `chat` object for LLM calls.
* It would automatically handle context window management and recursion limits (`max_steps`).
* User Experience:
  ```r
  agent <- Agent$new(chat)
  agent$run("Analyze this dataset")

2. Strict Tool Interface Current tool definitions are flexible, but an Agent needs strict contracts. I propose a Tool class that:
* Wraps R functions (e.g., read.csv, ggplot).
* Automatically generates the JSON schema required by OpenAI/Anthropic (extracting params from formals()).
* Handles execution errors gracefully, feeding them back to the LLM for self-correction.

3. Safety & Sandboxing (Crucial) Autonomy requires safety. The Agent would include:
* File System Jail: Restricting I/O to a specific subdirectory (e.g., ./agent_scratchpad/).
* Human-in-the-Loop: A confirm_execution = TRUE mode where the user approves tools before they run.

Implementation Details
I have spent time analyzing ellmer's internals (specifically during my work on PR #906 regarding chat history architecture) and believe this can be implemented as a clean layer on top of the existing providers.

GSoC 2026 Participation
I have drafted a complete 5-page Technical Specification (including architecture diagrams and a 12-week timeline) for building this feature.

I would love to champion this implementation as a Google Summer of Code 2026 project.

Question for Maintainers: Is ellmer (or the Tidyverse team) considering participating in GSoC this year?

If so, I am ready to share the full proposal immediately. If not, I am still keen to discuss this design for future community contributions!

New Feature Request : Custom metadata labels - Vertex A
body:
Hi Team,

Request your support to add Custom metadata label while accessing gemini models in Vertex AI.

Business Need:

(Source Reference : https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/multimodal/add-labels-to-api-calls)
What are labels?
A label is a key-value pair that you can assign to generateContent and streamGenerateContent API calls. They help you organize these calls and manage your costs at scale, with the granularity you need. You can attach a label to each call, then filter the calls based on their labels. Information about labels is forwarded to the billing system that lets you break down your billed charges by label. With built-in [billing reports](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/reports), you can filter and group costs by labels.

Common use cases for labels
Team or cost center labels: Add labels based on team or cost center to distinguish API calls owned by different teams (for example, team:research and team:analytics). You can use this type of label for cost accounting or budgeting.
Component labels: For example, component:redis, component:frontend, component:ingest, and component:dashboard.
Environment or stage labels: For example, environment:production and environment:test.
Ownership labels: Used to identify the teams that are responsible for operations, for example: team:shopping-cart.

R Code to access via REST API

```R
library(httr)
library(jsonlite)

# ---- STEP 1: Set your values ----
project_id <- "your-project-id"            # <-- Replace with your GCP project ID
location <- "us-central1"                  # <-- Replace with region (e.g., us-central1)
model_id <- "gemini-1.5-pro-preview-0409"  # <-- Replace with your model ID
response_method <- "generateContent"       # or "streamGenerateContent"

# Prompt and labels
prompt_text <- "What are the key benefits of using generative AI in financial services?"
label_key <- "env"
label_value <- "test"

# ---- STEP 2: Get access token from gcloud ----
access_token <- system("gcloud auth print-access-token", intern = TRUE)

# ---- STEP 3: Prepare request body ----
body <- list(
  contents = list(
    role = "USER",
    parts = list(text = prompt_text)
  ),
  labels = setNames(list(label_value), label_key)
)

# ---- STEP 4: Convert to JSON ----
json_body <- toJSON(body, auto_unbox = TRUE)

# ---- STEP 5: Make POST request ----
url <- sprintf("https://%s-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/%s/locations/%s/publishers/google/models/%s:%s",
               location, project_id, location, model_id, response_method)

res <- POST(
  url,
  add_headers(
    Authorization = paste("Bearer", access_token),
    `Content-Type` = "application/json; charset=utf-8"
  ),
  body = json_body
)

# ---- STEP 6: View the response ----
cat(content(res, "text", encoding = "UTF-8"))
```
